Definition: Whether the civil registration and digital ID systems are integrated
Comments: No integration between civil registration and ID system. World Bank 2021 noted 27% of population and a quarter of births remain unregistered. No CRVS-ID linkage has been established.
revision_notes: Original score (1, No integration, 2022) confirmed by the World Bank's 2022 Project Appraisal Document, which found civil registration and ID legislation not yet updated and no digital ID system in existence. Checked for more recent evidence: a UNICEF-supported interoperability pilot (since October 2023, Kirundo province) links civil registry offices with health facilities for real-time birth registration, but this connects civil registration to the health sector, not to a digital ID system. In May 2026 the Ministry of the Interior unveiled a new digital civil-registration platform tied to production of a biometric national ID, with the card's unique identifier intended to serve as a reference across other official documents; however, as of June 2026 this remains pre-launch, awaiting adoption of the enabling legal decree, so no operational CRVS-digital ID integration yet exists. Score confirmed at 1 (No integration).
revised_comments: Burundi has no operational integration between its civil registration system and a digital identity system. A new digital civil-registration platform linked to the planned biometric national identity card was unveiled by the Ministry of the Interior in May 2026, with the card's unique identifier intended to serve as a reference across other official documents, but the system remains pre-launch pending adoption of the enabling legal decree. Separately, since October 2023 UNICEF has supported an interoperability pilot between civil registry offices and health facilities in Kirundo province for real-time birth registration, but this links civil registration to the health sector rather than to a digital ID system.

Definition: Whether the ongoing management, maintenance and development of the ID system can be funded by sustainable domestic resources
Comments: Burundi's digital ID and digital transformation projects are primarily externally funded. The World Bank Digital Foundations Project (2022) provided a $50M IDA grant. Country described as dependent on external financial support.
revision_notes: Original score (1, Primarily dependent on external funding, 2022) based on the USD 50 million World Bank IDA grant for the Digital Foundations Project. Checked for more recent evidence: in February 2025 Burundi was in talks with the IFC on further digital-transformation collaboration and PPP financing, and by June 2026 Burundian officials were negotiating with India to adapt the India Stack model (UPI/Aadhaar-style architecture) for digital ID and payments, explicitly to reduce cost and reliance on proprietary foreign vendors -- itself evidence of continued reliance on external partners for core system design and financing. No evidence found of a shift to domestically funded operations or a dedicated, sustainable domestic budget line for the ID system. Score confirmed at 1.
revised_comments: Burundi's digital identity and civil registration modernisation remains primarily dependent on external funding and technical partnerships. The World Bank's Digital Foundations Project (a USD 50 million IDA grant approved in 2022, with total project cost of around USD 92 million) remains the principal financing vehicle. Burundi held further talks with the IFC in February 2025 on public-private partnership financing for its digital transformation agenda, and by June 2026 was negotiating with India to adapt the India Stack model for its national ID and payments infrastructure. No dedicated, sustainable domestic funding mechanism for the ID system has been established.

Definition: Whether the system collects biometric data and which modalities are collected (fingerprints, facial image, iris scans)
Comments: The new biometric CNI collects fingerprints, facial photograph, and eye colour data. The legacy paper CNI did not include biometrics. Biometric collection confirmed in pilot (11 communes) as of December 2023.
revision_notes: Original score (3, Facial/Iris, 2023) cited a December 2023 pilot demonstration in Gitega where the new biometric ID collected fingerprints, a facial photograph, and an 'eye colour' descriptive field (not an iris scan). Checked more recent evidence: a May 2026 Ministry of the Interior presentation of the finalised biometric ID system (still piloted in around a dozen communes, technically ready for production but awaiting an enabling decree) confirms fingerprint collection and reiterates a biometric design consistent with the 2023 pilot, without mentioning iris scanning specifically. No source confirms genuine iris biometric capture; 'eye colour' in the original comment appears to be a descriptive attribute rather than a biometric modality. Facial photograph capture, in addition to fingerprints, still supports a score of 3 on the given scale (which groups facial or iris capture together as exceeding 'fingerprints only'). Score confirmed at 3, with the comment corrected to remove the inaccurate iris reference.
revised_comments: Burundi's new biometric national identity card, still in pilot phase across roughly a dozen communes as of mid-2026 and awaiting the legal decree needed for nationwide rollout, is designed to collect fingerprints and a facial photograph, replacing the non-biometric legacy paper card. There is no confirmed evidence that iris scanning is used.

Definition: Whether the digital ID system is designed to be interoperable across government agencies and with other systems through APIs or data exchange protocols
Comments: No evidence of system interoperability. World Bank Digital Foundations Project (2022) noted Burundi's back-end systems are characterised by incompatible systems and standards. No foundational digital ID stack with interoperability has been deployed.
revision_notes: Original score (1, No, 2022) based on the World Bank's 2022 Project Appraisal Document, which found Burundi's e-government systems fragmented, running on incompatible standards, with no shared interoperability platform and no foundational digital ID stack. Checked for more recent evidence: the World Bank Digital Foundations Project is funding development of a national interoperability platform, PKI and data exchange layer, and by June 2026 Burundi was in talks with India to adapt the India Stack model to eventually link digital ID directly with instant payment rails. DPI Map (last updated January 2024) also records 'semantic interoperability' and 'real-time sharing' as not established for Burundi's data exchange system. As of mid-2026 the new biometric ID platform remains pre-launch, awaiting an enabling decree, and there is no evidence of live, operational cross-agency API-based interoperability. Score confirmed at 1 (No).
revised_comments: Burundi's digital identity system is not yet interoperable across government agencies. The national data exchange and interoperability platform being built under the World Bank-financed Digital Foundations Project remains under development, and the new biometric national ID system unveiled in May 2026 is still pre-launch, pending adoption of an enabling legal decree. Burundi is separately exploring adoption of India's India Stack architecture to eventually link digital identity with instant payment rails, but no operational, API-based data exchange currently exists between the ID system and other government systems.
